title: reading-notes-llm-inference-raja-singh
content:
TL;DR:
- Quick notes + to-dos from recent papers, blogs, and ICLR/NeurIPS talks relevant to production LLM serving. Focus on low-latency kernels, memory-friendly attention, quantization trade-offs, and evaluation ideas for rollout.

Papers / posts summarized (short):
1) FlashAttention (11/2020 paper, still highly relevant)
   - Key idea: IO-aware exact attention with block-wise fwd/bwd to avoid large intermediate memory. Great for long sequences and reduces peak memory vs naive matmul-based attention.
   - Production relevance: allows larger context at similar GPU memory. For serving, reduces OOMs for long prompt caching and makes batch packing easier.
   - Notes: benchmark on H100 vs A100 for our 16k-context models; check kernel availability in Triton and cuBLAS fallback.

2) Quantization-aware inference notes (various recent blogs/papers)
   - Mixed results: 4-bit quantization (e.g., GPTQ-style) gives big memory wins with some accuracy drop; A/B test needed for customer-facing LLMs.
   - Observation: some model families (decoder-only) tolerate aggressive quant; encoder-decoder often less forgiving on seq2seq tasks.
   - Production checklist: per-model eval set + quality regression alerts; auto-rollback on hallucination spike.

3) KV cache strategies (talks at ICLR 2025)
   - Dynamic vs static caching: dynamic prefix caching (per-user heuristics) can lower token compute for multi-turn chat.
   - Memory compaction: store cached keys/values in quantized format (int8 or 4-bit) with on-the-fly dequant when needed. Trade latency vs memory.
   - Action item: prototype a compact kv-cache store using 8-bit arrays and measure decode latency increase for 8k-length histories.

4) Grouped/Flash-style attention variants (emerging)
   - Promises lower compute for long-context by sparsifying queries or grouping heads. Might require model finetune or rearchitecting. Not immediate for hosted RL, but worth tracking for Dedicated customers with ultra-long contexts.

Practical experiments to run (short term):
- E1: FlashAttention kernel compatibility sweep on our inference container (ubuntu22 + cuda13)
  - Metrics: p99 latency, throughput tokens/s, peak GPU memory for prompt lengths [512, 2048, 8192].
  - Owners: @Aisha to run basic perf harness; @Raja to integrate into nightly perf job.

- E2: Quantization A/B on customer eval set (gpt-style 7B and 13B candidates)
  - Approach: generate outputs for 500 prompts -> automated eval (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-sim) + human spot-check for hallucination.
  - Metric thresholds: <2% relative drop in embedding-similarity, no increase in hallucination incidents >1%.
  - Linked ticket: JIRA INF-2345.

- E3: Compact KV cache prototype
  - Implementation note: store K/V in int8 with scale per-row; use CUDA kernel to dequant on-the-fly into float16 for matmul.
  - Risks: extra memcopy and dequant latency; might still be beneficial for very long contexts where memory savings enable batching.

Evaluation + rollout considerations:
- Always tie quantization/kv-cache changes to eval suites and an automated regression alert in Optimize. If rolling to Hosted, start with a canary group (10% traffic) and monitor output-quality metrics + customer complaints.
- Provide a Dedicated flag to opt-in to experimental kernels (customers who want max throughput can enable before we fully QA).

Conference takeaways (ICLR 2025 sessions I attended):
- "Memory-efficient attention" session: main message is software + kernel-level optimization still buys a lot before changing the model. Focus on reducing IO and peak live memory.
- "Serving at scale" panel: operators emphasize observability (token-level cost breakdown) and graceful degradation (fallback to smaller model variants). Aligns with Redwood product direction.

Notes-to-self / open questions:
- How much p99 hit does on-the-fly dequant (int8->fp16) cause at decode step for single-request low-latency workloads? Need microbenchmarks (1-token generation).
- Can we add an inference config flag that toggles per-layer quantization (e.g., keep first/last N layers in fp16) and run a matrix to find minimal quality drop?
- Should add a small section in the perf dashboard that shows kernel-level breakdown (attention vs matmul vs KV-copy) per model so we can attribute wins.

References / quick links:
- FlashAttention: https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04768
- GPTQ notes + repos (internal links pinned in confluence)
- Internal PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/482 (perf harness updates)
- JIRA: INF-2345 (quantization experiment tracking)

Next steps (this week):
- Send short summary to eng-applied-ml and eng-serving-runtime with proposed E1/E2 experiments (by Fri).
- Start FlashAttention kernel sweep on staging infra (queue on h100-dev pool).
- Draft an eval-run template for quantization A/B (embedding sim + hallucination heuristics).

Quick TODOs (inlined):
- [ ] Create perf job for p99 microbenchmarks (Raja)
- [ ] Coordinate GPU slots with infra (Aisha)
- [ ] Update perf dashboard to ingest kernel-level counters (follow-up with observability team)

Random jotting (notes to self):
- If decode token-level latency >16ms for single-token generation after dequant, probably too slow for hosted default. Consider Dedicated-opt-in.
- Long-term: quantify cost delta (tokens/$) for enabling 4-bit quantization across common workload mix (chat vs summarization).

End of notes.

(These are personal working notes — will refine into a short proposal once E1/E2 data is in.)
